topics.title: Cool stuff
topics.bodyHtml:
Safety

  • No editing on 'Playing' — the 'Playing' tab never lets you change a playlist, so an operator who's unsure or unpracticed can't accidentally break anything just by using it.
  • PIN lockout — set a PIN in Settings and both 'Edit Playlists' and 'Library' will ask for it before they open, if you want to keep them out of reach.
  • 10-minute revert — leave 'Edit Playlists' or 'Library' untouched for 10 minutes and the app quietly switches the display back to 'Playing' on its own — it doesn't start any playback, just brings that tab back to the front — so whoever finds it next isn't looking at an editing screen they didn't expect.

Handy features

  • Look ahead without losing your place — while something is playing, clicking another playlist opens it over the playing one, which stays live underneath with its waveform in view. Pick a track, see its waveform, and click in it to choose where to start; then the play button (or Enter, from the top of the track) switches to it. Click its title to make it the active playlist, ready at its first track without playing (you're asked first if something is playing), or double-click the title to start it straight away. Escape, ✕, or a click outside closes it with nothing changed.
  • Waveform seekbar — the waveform on the 'Playing' screen shows the shape of the verses and silences in the track, so you can click straight to the right spot when you need to.
  • Even loudness — recordings from different sources can be much louder or softer than each other. Settings → Playback can even them out as they play, track by track or album by album (an album moves as a whole, so its own quiet and loud parts stay as recorded), and any single track can be turned up or down in its details (✎). Evening out never turns a track up past its loudest moment; turning it up yourself can go further, which helps on small speakers, and the details say when its loudest moments may clip for an instant. Every player in the app follows the same levels, and the files themselves are never changed. To see each track's measured loudness, turn on 'Show loudness in Library' in the display settings (◐).
  • Stop — put a Stop wherever you need one in a playlist and give it a name, like "Stop for meditation." Playback pauses there and waits for a click to continue — no more prayers starting up while someone's teaching.
  • Split track — no need for Audacity. On the 'Library' tab, play a track to the point you want, click Split track, and edit the details for each half before saving them as two separate tracks.
  • Library cleanup — 'Find duplicates', on the 'Library' tab, goes through copies of the same recording one group at a time (the kind left by importing the same CDs more than once), with each copy's artwork and details side by side, the albums they come from below, and a player to compare them. Mark each copy Keep, Delete or Ignore; take a better name or artwork from a copy before it goes; and playlists that used a deleted copy switch to the one you keep. Settings → Library cleanup also lists tracks whose audio is missing and tracks that can't be played. Convert turns a format a browser can't play (Windows Media Audio, Apple Lossless, compressed AIFF) into an MP3 that plays everywhere, keeping the track in its playlists; Check again looks at each stored file afresh and repairs what it can (an AIFF an older version left at 0:00 comes back as WAV); nothing is removed without your say.
  • Tags that stay with the files — change a track's name, artist, album, track number or artwork, and the audio file itself is updated to match, so an exported copy or another music player shows the same thing. The audio is never re-encoded for this, and every other tag the file holds (year, genre, comments, lyrics…) is kept. Works for MP3, M4A, FLAC, Opus, Ogg, WAV and AIFF, and for WebM without artwork. When Standardize makes a file smaller, it copies all of the original's tags onto the new file. Portable exports also put a cover.jpg in each album folder. Importing a folder works the other way: its picture (cover.jpg, folder.jpg and the like, or the folder's only picture, or one in the folder above it) goes to any track that has none of its own, and into the track's file too.
  • Printable playlists — in 'Edit Playlists', the print button on a playlist (or on a folder, for every playlist in it) makes a page for planning a session with the teacher: each prayer's title and length in large type, and at every stop the time played so far, with the time still to come on the line after it. Print it, or save it as a PDF from the print dialog.
  • Side-by-side playlist editing — the 'Edit Playlists' screen's two-pane layout makes it easy to build a playlist while browsing your library right alongside it.
  • Export — two different formats, depending on what you need. One is a .zip meant purely for re-importing into 37 Player. The other unpacks into a plain folder structure any other player can use (volume adjustments and evening out stay behind in 37 Player — they aren't written into the files as ReplayGain tags):
music/artist/album/files
playlists/(your own folder structure)/playlist.m3u8

topics.title: Runs in a browser
topics.bodyHtml:
37 Player runs entirely in a browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, etc.) — there's nothing to install, and it works the same on Windows, Mac, Linux, or a Chromebook. Your library lives inside the browser too, in its own storage. For what that means — how it works without the internet, and how to keep the library safe — see 'Reliability'.

Because the library lives inside the browser, you won't find it as files on your disk (unless you're kind of a hacker-type). To get your music back out as ordinary files — for another player, or just to look through — use 'Import / Export' → Export and choose Portable. It unpacks into a structure like this:

/music/New Kadampa Tradition/Heart Jewel/files
/music/New Kadampa Tradition/OSG/files
/music/Silence/Silence/files
/playlists/action tantra/avalokiteshvara sadhana.m3u8
/playlists/action tantra/medicine buddha sadhana.m3u8

That structure can be useful to other programs, and it can also be imported back into 37 Player — but 37 Player itself always plays from within the browser's own storage, never directly from an exported copy.

{{setup-locally}}

topics.title: Reliability
topics.bodyHtml:
37 Player is built to be dependable in the middle of a session: once it's set up, it doesn't need the internet, and your library is kept right there on the computer. This page explains where the library lives, what could erase it, and how to protect it — and suggests two short exercises that prove all of this to yourself before you rely on it at an event.

Where your library lives

Everything you put into 37 Player — the audio, playlists, stops and silences, notes, artwork, and every edit — is stored inside the browser, in a database that every browser has built in, called IndexedDB. It isn't a folder of files you can open; it's tucked away in the browser's own storage, alongside its settings and history.

That storage is kept separately for each browser and each website address. Chrome and Safari on the same computer each have their own library; so do the website and a 37-player.html file opened from disk. (See 'Multiple instances'.)

Keeping everything inside the browser is what makes 37 Player quick and able to work offline. The other side of it is that the library is only as safe as the browser's storage — which is why backups matter.

Working offline

After the first visit, 37 Player doesn't need the internet at all. The browser keeps its own copy of the app, and the library is already on the computer, so you can open 37 Player and run a whole session with no connection.

Only a few things use the internet:

  • the very first visit, to load the app;
  • a shared library, to sync;
  • checking for and installing updates. Click the version number at the top (v1.3…) to check. On a phone, it's under ☰. If there's a newer version, Update installs it and reloads 37 Player. The library stays as it is, but playback stops, so don't do it mid-session.

A copy opened from a file (such as the 37-player.html in your backup folder) doesn't need the internet even the first time — only for updates.

What can erase the library — and what protects it

  • Clearing the browser's data. "Clear browsing data", clearing history with site data included, or cleanup tools such as CleanMyMac or CCleaner erase it on the spot. Nothing inside the browser can prevent that; only a backup protects against it.
  • The browser making room. When the disk gets very full, a browser may delete a website's storage to free up space — unless that storage has been marked persistent. 37 Player asks for this every time it starts, and installing it as an app makes it much more likely to be granted (see 'Setup'). Firefox may ask you directly — choose Allow. To check, open Settings (⚙, on 'Edit Playlists' or 'Library') → Library info → Storage.
  • Safari's one-week rule. Safari erases a website's storage after seven days of using Safari without visiting that site. Opening 37 Player regularly avoids it. So does adding it to the Dock (Safari → File → Add to Dock, macOS Sonoma or later) or to the Home Screen on an iPhone or iPad: opening that app counts as a visit. Note that the Dock or Home Screen app keeps its own separate library.
  • Private or incognito windows keep nothing once they're closed. Never build a library in one.
  • Uninstalling or resetting the browser, deleting the browser's user profile, or the computer failing or being lost.

For everything on that list, the real protection is a backup. In Chrome, Edge, and other browsers built on the same engine, backups to a folder happen automatically (in Brave, first turn on "File System Access API" at brave://flags). In Firefox and Safari, and on phones and tablets, backups are manual. See 'Backing up'.

If the computer freezes or loses power

A crash at the moment 37 Player is saving can damage part of the browser's storage. 37 Player keeps a spare copy of the library's list of tracks and playlists, a few minutes behind at most, and uses it by itself if the main one can't be read — anything changed in those last few minutes may need doing again.

If neither can be read, 37 Player says so when it starts, and changes nothing until you choose:

  • Restore from your backup folder (or a backup file). Audio still stored in the browser is kept, and any that the backup doesn't know about — added since it was made — can be added back as tracks afterwards.
  • Rebuild the tracks from the audio still stored here. The audio is stored separately and usually survives; each track gets its name, artist, album and artwork from the file itself. Playlists can't be rebuilt this way, so backups to your backup folder pause until you've restored from it (or chosen to replace it).

Don't clear the browser's data in this situation — that would erase the audio that's still there.

Try it: run with no internet

Worth doing once, so there are no surprises at an event:

  1. Make or import a small library — a few tracks and one playlist are plenty.
  2. Close 37 Player, then open it again while still online. (This makes sure the browser has kept its copy of the app.)
  3. Turn off Wi-Fi, and unplug any network cable.
  4. Close 37 Player, open it again, and play the playlist.

It should open and play exactly as before. Turn Wi-Fi back on when you're done.

Try it: restore from a backup

The surest way to trust a backup is to restore from one. With automatic backups it takes a minute or two:

  1. Check that the button at the top says ✓ Backed up. Anything not yet backed up would be lost.
  2. Clear 37 Player's data — only 37 Player's, not the whole browser's (see below).
  3. Open 37 Player again, while online: clearing its data also removes the browser's saved copy of the app, so this one visit needs the internet. It starts as if new, and its setup appears.
  4. Choose the same backup folder, and pick Restore this backup. Everything comes back, and backups carry on as before.

With manual backups (Firefox, Safari), first click Back up library and keep the downloaded file in a folder of its own. After clearing, use 'Import / Export' → Restore backup from folder and choose that folder.

Clearing only 37 Player's data

The browser's general "Clear browsing data" command clears every website — you'd be signed out of email and lose saved settings everywhere. Instead, clear just 37 Player's site, with its page open in an ordinary browser window:

  • Chrome, Edge, Brave: click the icon at the left end of the address bar → Site settings → Delete data. (An installed 37 Player app shares its data with the website, so this clears both.)
  • Firefox: click the padlock at the left end of the address bar → Clear cookies and site data…
  • Safari on a Mac: Safari → Settings → Privacy → Manage Website Data…; search for the site, select it, and click Remove.
  • iPhone or iPad: Settings → Safari (on newer versions, Settings → Apps → Safari) → Advanced → Website Data; find the site and swipe left to delete it.

topics.title: Multiple instances
topics.bodyHtml:
37 Player's library lives inside the browser, and the browser keeps a separate storage area for each website address. So whether two copies of 37 Player share one library or have two different libraries depends on where they're running.

Several windows or tabs, same website, same browser

Windows and tabs that open 37 Player from the same website address (for example 37player.com) in the same browser all use one and the same library. So do the website and an installed 37 Player app in Chrome or Edge. They also share the same backup folder.

They stay in step with each other: a change made in one window — renaming a playlist, adding a prayer, deleting a track — appears in the others within a moment. If a window has a dialog open at the time, it catches up as soon as the dialog closes. So it's fine to play in one window and edit the same playlist in another, even mid-session: whatever is playing carries on, and the changes take effect when it finishes.

In the rare case that two windows change the library at almost the same instant, the second one is told its change couldn't be saved and shows the current library, so you can simply redo it — nothing is silently overwritten.

Each window plays its own audio, so playing in two windows at once means two sounds at once.

Different browsers

Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari each keep their own storage, so each has its own separate library, even on the same computer and at the same website address. The same goes for:

  • different browser profiles (for example two people's profiles in Chrome);
  • private or incognito windows — their library is also erased when the window closes;
  • different computers;
  • a copy opened from a file, such as app/index.html in the backup folder;
  • an app added to the Home Screen on an iPhone or iPad, which is kept separate from Safari;
  • a slightly different address, such as with or without "www", or "http" instead of "https".

Changes in one of these never appear in another.

Moving a library from one to another

  • With a backup folder: in the copy you want to use, choose that backup folder in setup (or Settings) and pick Restore this backup. The folder then belongs to that copy, and backups continue there.
  • Without one: in the old copy use 'Import / Export' → Export, then in the new copy 'Import / Export' → Import.

Each separate library needs its own backup folder. If two of them are set to the same folder, 37 Player notices and shows Backup paused rather than letting them overwrite each other — see the 'Backing up' topic.

topics.title: Setup
topics.bodyHtml:
The first time 37 Player opens, it asks for your language, then walks you through what matters on the device and browser you're using. For why these steps matter, see 'Reliability'.

Choose one home for your library

Your library lives in one browser, at one address, so decide where 37 Player will live and stay with it:

  • One browser. Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari each keep their own library. So do two installations of the same browser: on Linux, for example, a Flatpak Chrome and a Chrome installed from a .deb package are two separate browsers.
  • One address. The website (37player.com) and a 37-player.html file opened from your disk are separate libraries, with separate backups.

Settings → Library info shows where the library you're looking at lives. To move a library somewhere else later, see 'Multiple instances'.

Which browser

Chrome or Edge on a computer (Windows, Mac, Linux or Chromebook) is the best home: they keep a backup folder up to date by themselves. Most browsers built on the same engine can too; in Brave, first turn on "File System Access API" at brave://flags.

In Firefox or Safari on a computer, 37 Player works, but backups are files you save yourself. If you have Chrome or Edge, it's easiest to switch before adding anything, because a library doesn't move from one browser to another by itself. The welcome offers to copy the address so you can paste it into Chrome or Edge.

Choose a backup folder

In Chrome, Edge and similar browsers, the welcome asks for a backup folder. Create a new, empty folder and choose it: 37 Player then keeps it up to date by itself, and also keeps a copy of 37 Player itself there (37-player.html). If your library is ever lost, open 37 Player again and choose that folder to bring everything back. In other browsers, and on phones and tablets, backups are manual. See 'Backing up'.

iPad and iPhone: the Home Screen first

On an iPad or iPhone, Safari erases a website's data after 7 days without a visit. Added to the Home Screen, 37 Player keeps its library. The Home Screen app has a library of its own, separate from Safari's, so add it before importing anything. See 'Phones and tablets' for the steps.

Android: install it as an app

On Android, the welcome offers to install 37 Player as an app (or use Chrome's ⋮ menu → Add to Home screen). Chrome then keeps the library safe rather than clearing it when space runs low. The app and the website share one library, so it can be done at any time.

On a computer, installing is optional

In Chrome or Edge on a computer, 37 Player can also be installed as an app (the install icon in the address bar, or the ⋮ menu). It opens in a window of its own, with its own icon, and shares the website's library. Browsers are more likely to mark an installed app's storage persistent, protected from being cleared when the disk fills up. 37 Player asks for persistent storage every time it starts; if the browser shows a prompt about it, choose Allow. To check whether it's been granted, open Settings → Library info.

Opening audio files with 37 Player

Installed as an app, 37 Player can open audio files from outside it:

  • On a computer (Chrome, Edge or Brave): it's offered under Open with for MP3, M4A, WAV, FLAC and the other audio types. It can be made the default for a type the usual way: Default apps on Windows, Get Info → Open with → Change All on a Mac, or the file manager's settings on Linux. The first time, the browser asks once whether to allow it.
  • On Android: it's in the Share menu, so a recording can be shared to it from Files, a chat, or a recorder app.

Either way, 37 Player asks: Play it now (in a little player of its own; the library stays as it is, and anything playing in 37 Player is paused first), Import (the usual import, behind the PIN), or Play and import (imported, then played from the Library). This isn't possible on an iPad or iPhone, in Safari on a Mac, or in Firefox.

The new address

37 Player moved from player.37dakinis.net to 37player.com in October 2026. Because the browser keeps a library separately for each address, a device that used the old address still has its library there. The old address shows 37 Player has moved in the top bar, with the way across for the open library: a shared library is simply joined again at 37player.com; any other library is exported there and imported at 37player.com, or restored from its backup folder. On an iPad or phone, the Home Screen app is then removed and added again from the new address.

topics.title: iTunes / Music.app
topics.bodyHtml:
How 37 Player works alongside Music.app on a Mac and iTunes on Windows: bringing a library in, taking one back out, and why standardizing matters there.

Importing

37 Player can bring in a whole Music.app or iTunes library in one go — the audio, and every playlist inside its playlist folders.

1. Export the library file. In Music.app (or iTunes), choose File → Library → Export Library… and save the file into the folder that holds your music:

  • Music.app: the Media folder, usually in your Music folder under Music → Media.
  • iTunes on Windows: the iTunes Media folder, usually in your Music folder under iTunes → iTunes Media.

Keep the name it suggests (Library.xml). That one file lists every playlist and where each of its tracks is.

2. Import the folder. In 37 Player, open 'Import / Export', choose Import a folder…, and pick that same folder. 37 Player reads the library file along with the audio, and the usual review appears: how many tracks are new, and which playlist entries couldn't be found. Choose Import, and the playlists appear in 'Edit Playlists' in the same folders they had in Music.app.

Good to know:

  • Everything in the folder is imported, not just the tracks your playlists use. To bring in less, pick a smaller folder (one artist, say) — playlists still come in, with anything outside that folder listed as missing.
  • Apple's own lists (Library, Music, Downloaded and the like) are left out. A smart playlist comes in as the tracks it held when you exported — it doesn't keep updating.
  • A track that can't be found — never downloaded (streamed from Apple Music, or left in the cloud), or outside the folder you picked — leaves a Stop in its place in the playlist, named "MISSING TRACK: title — album", so playback halts right there instead of quietly skipping it, and the playlist is flagged. Once the track is in the library, put it in where the Stop is, and remove the Stop.
  • AIFF files (.aif), common in older iTunes libraries, come in as WAV, since most browsers can't play AIFF. The sound is identical, and the name, artist, album and artwork come along.
  • Older iTunes Store purchases protected against copying (.m4p files) can't be played in a browser.
  • Files a browser can't play — Windows Media Audio (.wma), Apple Lossless (ALAC, inside an .m4a) outside Safari, compressed AIFF and a few others — are converted to MP3 as they come in, so they play everywhere and keep their place in the playlists. 37 Player then asks whether to keep the originals too, for a later export (a portable export takes the original), showing how much room they take; Settings → Library cleanup can discard them later. Converting needs 37 Player's converter, which it fetches by itself (about 31 MB, once) and keeps, so it works offline afterwards; it waits while anything is playing. Without the converter (no internet the first time, say), such files come in marked "Can't be played", with Convert them now for later.
  • Your music doesn't have to be organized the way Music.app keeps it. Tracks are found by their folder names and file name, and if a file has moved, by its name and size.
  • Single playlists work too: a playlist exported on its own (File → Library → Export Playlist…, as an .m3u file), or an .m3u, .m3u8 or .xspf (VLC) from another player. Put it in the music folder and import the folder. ('Importing playlists' explains where playlists end up.)

Exporting

To take a library from 37 Player into Music.app or iTunes, use 'Import / Export' → Export and choose Portable. It unpacks into a music folder (artist / album / tracks) and a playlists folder of .m3u8 files.

  • The audio: in Music.app, choose File → Import… and pick the music folder.
  • The playlists: choose File → Library → Import Playlist… and pick each .m3u8 file. Music.app doesn't recreate folders from these, so a playlist lands at the top level; drag it into a playlist folder afterwards if you want one.

Every track keeps its name, artist, album, track number and artwork, since 37 Player writes those into the files themselves.

Volume adjustments made in 37 Player, and its evening out, don't come along: they aren't written into the files as ReplayGain tags, so Music.app plays each file at its own level. Music.app's own Sound Check (in its Playback settings) evens tracks out in a similar way.

Why standardize for Music.app and iTunes

Music.app and iTunes play one track straight into the next — but only smoothly when the two are alike. When the next track is a different file type (MP3 after AAC), or has a different sample rate (44.1 kHz after 48 kHz, say) or a different number of channels (mono after stereo), the player has to reset its audio output between them, and you hear a click, dropout, short gap, or worse.

37 Player itself doesn't have this problem, so there's no need to change the library for it. Instead, when exporting with Portable, tick Convert to the preferred format: every file in the export comes out alike, and the library stays as it is. For a stricter match, set the preferred format (Settings → File format) to Best for Apple (AAC, 44.1 kHz, stereo), or choose your own under Custom.

The library's file format

Settings → File format sets one preferred format for the library — Standard (MP3 192k, recommended), Best for Apple, Very small, Lossless (FLAC, not recommended: much larger, with no difference you can hear), or Custom — and which files are converted to it:

  • Don't touch my files: nothing is changed. A file this browser can't play still gets a playable copy, and its original is kept too.
  • Reduce uncompressed audio (recommended): WAV and AIFF files are converted as they come in.
  • Choose the rules: uncompressed audio, a bitrate above a limit, a sample rate or channel count other than the preferred format's, or less widely playable types (Opus, Ogg, WebM).

The page says what the settings would mean for the library as it is ("12 tracks would be converted…"). Converting them is in Settings → Library cleanup → Convert to the preferred format, with Convert them now and the list of those tracks (name, album, type, size, sample rate, bit rate, channels). In a shared library these settings belong to the library, so a change on one device applies on all of them, and a file about to be converted is never sent before its converted version is ready.

Videos (a recorded teaching, say) can come in too: 37 Player asks whether to take their sound as audio tracks. The video itself isn't kept.

topics.title: Importing playlists
topics.bodyHtml:
Playlists from other players come in along with their audio: choose the folder that holds both, in 'Import / Export' → Choose a folder… (or a .zip of it, with Choose a .zip file…).

What's read as a playlist

  • .m3u and .m3u8 files, from almost any player — and from 37 Player's own Portable export.
  • .xspf files, from VLC and others.
  • Library.xml, exported from Music.app or iTunes (File → Library → Export Library…) — every playlist in it, in its playlist folders. See 'iTunes / Music.app'.

A playlist file can be anywhere in the folder you choose. Its tracks are found wherever they are in that folder too — by where the playlist says they are, or, when that's a path on another computer, by the last few folder names and the file name. A track that can't be found leaves a Stop named "MISSING TRACK: …" in its place, and the playlist is flagged.

Playlists with missing audio: when some playlists here refer to audio that isn't in the folder (old playlist files left behind, say), the review says how many, lists them with how much of each was found, and asks: import all of them (each missing track becomes a Stop), only the ones with all their audio, or no playlists, only the audio. It starts at "all" while every such playlist found at least half its tracks, and otherwise at "only the ones with all their audio". When every playlist is complete, nothing is asked.

Only what the playlists use: everything in the folder is imported unless you say otherwise. When the folder has playlists, the review before importing offers Import only tracks that are in playlists (off to begin with) — handy for bringing in a friend's session playlists without their whole music collection.

Where the playlists end up

Playlists keep the folders they're in, as folders in 'Edit Playlists' — counted from the folder you chose:

  • Music/Morning.m3u8 → Morning, at the top level
  • Music/Pujas/Heruka.m3u8 → Pujas → Heruka
  • Music/Source Albums/Heart Jewel/Heart Jewel.m3u8 → Source Albums → Heart Jewel → Heart Jewel

That last one is the thing to watch: a playlist saved beside its album's audio brings the album's folders along as playlist folders.

A folder called "playlists" (any capitalization, at any depth) changes that: it and everything above it are left out, and only the folders beneath it are kept.

  • Music/PLAYLISTS/Kangso.xspf → Kangso, at the top level
  • Music/Playlists/Festivals/Spring/Day 1.m3u8 → Festivals → Spring → Day 1

So for the tidiest result, gather the playlist files into a "playlists" folder, arranged the way you'd like them to appear. 37 Player's Portable export always does this, so importing one gives back the same folders you had.

Playlists from Music.app's Library.xml are the exception: they keep the playlist folders they had in Music.app.

Folders as playlists

A folder with no playlist files in it can still come in as playlists. The review before importing offers Make a playlist of each folder — ticked to begin with when the folder has no playlists of its own, unticked when it does. Each folder holding audio becomes a playlist named after it, inside playlist folders arranged like the folders you chose, counting the chosen folder itself:

  • Pujas/Heruka/… and Pujas/Tara/… → Pujas → Heruka, and Pujas → Tara
  • Heart Jewel/… on its own → one playlist, Heart Jewel, at the top level
  • Teachings/Intro.mp3 beside Teachings/Day 1/… → Teachings → Teachings (the loose tracks) and Teachings → Day 1

Tracks are in track-number order, then by file name ("2" before "10"); a track with no number comes after the numbered ones. Since these playlists use every file, this and Import only tracks that are in playlists can't both be on.

Stopping an import part-way

Stop during an import doesn't throw anything away: the audio already in stays in. A short dialog says how far it got and how many playlists have all their tracks so far, and offers to make the complete playlists, all of them (tracks not imported yet become Stops, and the playlist is flagged), or none — or to carry on importing from where it stopped. Importing the same folder again later brings in the rest: what's already in is recognized, and a playlist made the first time is offered for Replace.

When a playlist is already here

A playlist with the same name, in the same folder, as one already in 'Edit Playlists' (from a playlist file, or a folder made into a playlist) is listed for review before anything is imported: Replace it (the usual choice when bringing in a newer version), Skip it, or Import as new alongside it.

topics.title: Backing up
topics.bodyHtml:
37 Player keeps your whole library inside the browser, and several everyday things can erase it there — clearing the browser's data above all (see 'Reliability'). The only real protection is a copy outside the browser, as ordinary files: a backup.

Automatic backups (Chrome, Edge, and similar browsers on a computer)

In Chrome or Edge on a computer (Windows, Mac, Linux, or Chromebook), 37 Player can keep a backup folder up to date by itself, a few seconds after every change. Most other browsers built on the same engine can too; in Brave, first turn on "File System Access API" at brave://flags.

  • Setting it up: the first time 37 Player starts, it asks for a backup folder. Create a new, empty folder and choose it — not your existing music folder. You can change it later in Settings. If Chrome asks whether 37 Player may keep access to the folder, choose Allow on every visit; otherwise it will ask again each time you open 37 Player (the button at the top will say Resume backups — click it to continue).
  • A synced folder (Dropbox, Google Drive, Syncthing, or similar) also gives you a copy off this computer.
  • The button at the top shows how things stand, on every tab: ✓ Backed up when all is well, Backing up… while it catches up.

Manual backups (other browsers, phones, and tablets)

Firefox, Safari, and browsers on phones and tablets can't write to a folder, so backups there are manual — at your own risk. When the library has changes that haven't been backed up, a Back up library button appears at the top: amber at first, red after an hour. Clicking it downloads a backup file; keep it somewhere safe. The first one is a full backup of everything. After that you can choose between backing up just the changes since the full backup — usually tiny and quick — or a new full backup; 37 Player shows the size of each, and recommends a new full backup once the changes grow past half its size. Keep your backup files together in one folder — for example 37 Player backups in your Music folder: to restore, use 'Import / Export' → Restore backup from folder and choose that folder, and 37 Player puts the newest full backup and its latest changes together for you.

Browsers save downloads to their Downloads folder unless told otherwise, and 37 Player can't choose the folder for them. So set your browser to ask where to save — in Firefox, Settings → General → Always ask you where to save files; in Safari, Settings → General → File download location → Ask for each download — then choose your backups folder once, and the browser remembers it next time.

It's also worth keeping a copy of 37 Player itself in that folder, so your backups never depend on the website: download 37-player.html from 37player.com (37 Player offers it during setup, too). Opened from the file, it keeps a library of its own — restore into it from your backups. When you leave 'Edit Playlists' or 'Library' with changes that haven't been backed up, 37 Player also asks whether to back up first.

Anyone can back up, even without the PIN — a backup never changes the library.

What's in the backup folder

  • Library - do not touch — the library itself. Please don't edit, rename, or rearrange anything in it; 37 Player relies on it exactly as it is. Its files are named by internal ID, not by title.
  • contents.csv — a list of every track, with its artist, album, name, and playlists. Open it in any spreadsheet program to find a particular recording.
  • 37-player.html — 37 Player itself, for running without the website (see below).
  • README.txt — a short explanation, for anyone who comes across the folder.

The backup is a mirror, not a history: something deleted in 37 Player is removed from the backup too. For a snapshot you can go back to, use 'Import / Export' → Export now and then, and keep that file somewhere else.

Devices in a shared library

A device in a shared library doesn't need backups of its own: the shared library keeps everything, and 37 Player stops asking once everything on the device has reached it. One computer that keeps a backup folder is still worth having, for mistakes that reach everyone. See 'Shared library'.

Restoring

If the browser's data is ever cleared, 37 Player starts as if new, and its setup appears again. Choose the same backup folder and pick Restore this backup — everything comes back, and backups carry on in that folder.

You can also restore at any time, in any browser, from 'Import / Export' → Restore backup from folder.

One folder, one copy of 37 Player

Each copy of 37 Player — in a particular browser, on a particular computer — has its own library. If two copies back up to the same folder (for example, two computers sharing a synced folder), each would keep replacing the other's library. So when 37 Player finds that another copy has taken over its backup folder, it stops and shows Backup paused; click it to choose what to do. Restoring from a folder hands it over to the copy that restored it.

Running without the website

As soon as you choose a backup folder, 37 Player puts a copy of itself there: 37-player.html. Open it in Chrome or Edge to run 37 Player without the website or an internet connection. If your backup was made from the website, the copy may start with an empty library of its own — restore from the same folder as described above.

That copy keeps itself up to date: when a newer version is published and there's an internet connection, it shows an Update button at the top. Updating keeps your library exactly as it is. Keep the file in its backup folder — that's what lets it update itself. Chrome or Edge on a computer only.

topics.title: Shared library
topics.bodyHtml:
A shared library keeps the same tracks and playlists on several devices: the rooms of a Center, or your own computer, phone and tablet. A change made on any of them, such as a new playlist, a renamed track or a tweak on the iPad, reaches the others by itself within a few minutes.

Joining

You need a join code from whoever runs your shared library. Enter it with a name for this device (for example "Temple iPad"), either in the welcome when 37 Player first opens (Join a shared library) or later in Settings → Shared library, and choose Join.

To bring only some of the shared library to this device, tick Bring only the playlists I choose (partial sync) beside the code. Nothing moves yet: the next step says how much would travel either way, with partial sync first, and you choose there. Partial sync can also be turned on or off later. See 'Partial sync' below.

  • A device with nothing in it yet simply receives the shared library.
  • A device that already has a library asks first. Each choice says what it removes, sends and downloads. Use the shared library here replaces what's on this device with the shared one, so anything only on this device is removed. Combine them (the suggested choice, since it loses nothing) adds this device's tracks and playlists to the shared library, which is how the first device fills an empty shared library. A recording this device imported separately (so 37 Player knows it by a different ID) is matched to the shared copy by its name, album, artist and length, so combining doesn't create duplicates. Folders and playlists work the same way: a folder or playlist with the same name in the same place becomes one with the shared one, such as the Archive folder every new library starts with. If a playlist's tracks differ, this device's version is kept beside the shared one as "Name (device name)", marked ⚠.

Before anything moves, 37 Player says how much joining will download or send (for example "about 2.1 GB"). On mobile data or a slow connection, you can cancel and join later.

The tracks' details and playlists arrive straight away, on every device. The audio follows in the background, shown in the bar along the bottom. A track that hasn't arrived yet is fetched the moment it's played. While anything is playing, sending and receiving pause between files so the sound stays clean, and pick up again when it stops. While the first device is still sending its audio, the others show how many files are still on their way, and pick them up as they arrive. A large library takes a while the first time; after that, only what changed travels.

On Google Drive

A shared library can also live in a folder of your Google Drive. In Settings → Shared library (or the welcome's join step), choose Use Google Drive… and sign in with Google. 37 Player then shows the 37 Player libraries in that Google Drive: choose one to join, or Make a new library on Google Drive. It appears in your Drive as a folder called "37 Player – " and the library's name.

  • Every device that shares it signs in with the same Google account, a Center's account, say. Sharing one Drive library between several people's own Google accounts isn't possible yet.
  • 37 Player sees only what it made in that Google Drive, nothing else.
  • Everything else works the same: what's on each device, reviewing changes, receiving updates only, and leaving.
  • If Google asks you to sign in again (the sign-in was removed in your Google account, say, or the device went unused for months), the button at the top says Sign in to Google. It takes you to Settings → Shared library and Sign in to Google again.
  • Leave the folder alone in Drive: don't move or rename what's inside it. Moving the folder itself, or renaming it, is fine.

Day to day

There's nothing to do. 37 Player checks a few seconds after every change, every few minutes while it's open, and whenever it comes back on screen. Sync now in Settings does it at once. Settings also shows when this device last checked, and whether it's up to date, still updating (downloading or sending audio), or waiting for files from other devices that haven't sent them yet.

  • Working offline is fine: everything plays from this device as always, and changes are sent the next time it's online.
  • Each device keeps its own settings: display, PIN, backups and volume aren't shared.
  • The shared library is this device's backup. Once everything on a device has reached the shared library, the Back up library button at the top reads In sync, and 37 Player stops reminding you to back up. Until then (just after a change, or while audio is being sent), it says Syncing…. Tapping In sync still lets you save a backup on this device: it opens with Up to date, then the usual backup choices.
  • Who keeps backups. A shared library still needs one device that backs it up: it protects against losing a device, but not against a mistake, because a mistake is shared too. A computer with Chrome or Edge and a backup folder (see 'Backing up') does it by itself, and every device shows when it last did, for example "Backed up by Gen's laptop, today" (on the button's tooltip, and in Settings → Backups and Shared library).

If a device loses its library

If a device's browser data is cleared, or you want to undo a mess on one device, don't restore an old backup into it: join the shared library again, and choose Use the shared library here. That brings back everything as it is now, with everyone's latest changes.

Restoring a backup on a device that's in a shared library offers Get the current shared library for this reason. Restoring an older backup there instead first leaves the shared library, because otherwise everything deleted since the backup was made would come back for everyone. A backup made on a device in a shared library says so when it's restored, and suggests joining that shared library instead.

When two devices change the same thing

37 Player compares each device's changes with the last version they both had, so most changes simply combine. A rename on one device and new artwork on another both survive, and so do two different playlists edited at the same time.

  • The same playlist's tracks changed on two devices before they synced: both versions are kept. The shared one keeps its name; the other appears beside it as "Name (device name)", marked ⚠. Look at both, keep the one you want, and delete the other.
  • The same detail of a track changed on both (the same track renamed differently, say): the version that reached the shared library first wins.
  • Deleted on one device but edited on another: the edited one is kept. A track still used in a playlist is never deleted.

Tracks that haven't arrived yet

A track whose audio isn't on this device yet shows its name in bold, with the reason under it:

  • "On its way from the shared library" means the shared library has the audio, and it's downloading. On Playing, Get them now above the list fetches a playlist's missing tracks straight away, even while something plays.
  • "Waiting for Office laptop to send it" means the device that added the track hasn't sent its audio yet, perhaps because it was closed too soon. It arrives once that device is open and online again.

Playing also says above the list how many of the playlist's tracks can't play yet, so check before a session starts.

Pressing play on a track that's on its way fetches it at once. If it arrives within a few seconds, it plays. If not, a message says it's still coming. Press play again once it's here. It never starts by itself later, so it can't interrupt whatever you've moved on to.

While 37 Player is sending audio, the bar along the bottom says so. Keep it open until that finishes. Closing the window asks first. Closing a laptop's lid can't be caught, so wait for the bar to finish before you close it.

Phones and tablets

A phone or tablet stops 37 Player soon after its screen locks, which pauses a big first sync. On a phone or tablet, Settings → Shared library has a Keep syncing with the screen off switch, which stays as you set it. While it's on, whenever there's something to send or receive and nothing is playing, 37 Player keeps going by quietly playing silence, with the progress on the lock screen, until everything has arrived. Playing always comes first: syncing waits while a session plays and carries on by itself the moment it stops, even with the screen locked. The lock screen's pause button stops it until you next open 37 Player or play something. It's best done plugged in.

Sharing uses mobile data like any other connection, because a shared library only works when every device keeps it complete. The one big transfer is when a device joins, and the join screen says how much that will be before it starts.

Reviewing changes before they sync

To decide for yourself what comes and goes, turn on Review changes before syncing in Settings → Shared library. Nothing then changes on this device or in the shared library until you say so. 37 Player still checks, and when this device and the shared library differ, a button at the top says so, such as 3 shared changes. Tap it (or Review changes… in Settings, which appears while this is on) to see the list.

Each row is one difference: a folder or playlist, a track, or the order of things inside a folder. The left side says what this device has, and the right side says what the shared library has. The arrow between them says which version wins:

  • → Send: this device's version goes to the shared library.
  • ← Take: the shared library's version comes here.
  • ✕ Skip: leave both as they are for now. The row comes up again next time.

Tap an arrow to change it. Each row starts with a suggestion: send what changed here, take what changed in the shared library. A row changed in both places is shown in red with ?, and you choose. Synchronize does what the arrows say, and it waits until every ? is decided.

New tracks are listed under the playlist that uses them. If you take or send a playlist, its new tracks have to come along, so their arrows are locked, with a note saying which playlist needs them. Skip the playlist and they unlock.

If anything changes while the list is open (someone else syncs, say), Synchronize first shows the updated list, keeping your choices where nothing changed. Check it, then press Synchronize again.

What's on this device

What's on this device… in Settings → Shared library shows the whole shared library, with a tick on everything that's on this device and the size of each folder and playlist. The total at the top says how much of the shared library this device holds.

  • Tick a playlist or folder to bring it here; untick it to take it off this device. The shared library keeps it, and so do the other devices. A track used by two playlists stays while either is ticked.
  • Nothing changes until Apply. The bar at the bottom says what Apply will do, for example "Brings 12 tracks (840 MB to download) · Takes 3 tracks off this device".
  • Albums, below the playlists, list every album in the shared library. Tick one to bring its tracks here, for example to make playlists from them, without bringing any playlist. An album shows as ticked when all its tracks will be here, and partly ticked when some come with a playlist.
  • Folders open and close by their arrow or their name; the box beside them ticks everything inside.
  • Cancel leaves everything as it was.

Everything, or only what you choose

Under On this device in Settings → Shared library:

  • Everything in the shared library (the usual choice): everything comes here and stays in step. A Center's playback computers and iPads, or your own phone and laptop, work this way, with nothing to think about. Unticking something in What's on this device asks first, then switches the device to the other choice.
  • Only what I choose: this device holds what's ticked in What's on this device. What it holds stays in step both ways, including new tracks added to its playlists elsewhere. Good for a small iPad, a laptop for one retreat, or helping with a few of a Center's playlists from home.
  • New playlists from other devices wait for you, marked New in What's on this device; the button at the top says how many, for example 2 new in the shared library, and opens it. Looking is enough to clear the count: they stay marked New while you look, and you don't have to bring them. Turn on New playlists from other devices come here by themselves to have them arrive on their own (what you've unticked stays off).
  • Deleting asks which you mean. Deleting a folder, playlist or track offers Remove from this device (the shared library keeps it, and What's on this device can bring it back) or Delete everywhere (it's deleted from the shared library and every device). Anything that disappears from this device some other way, such as through Library cleanup, counts as removed from this device. Only Delete everywhere deletes from the shared library.
  • Choosing Everything again brings the whole shared library here. 37 Player says how much that is first.

When joining, tick Bring only the playlists I choose beside the join code for Only what I choose. Everything already on the device joins the shared library, and What's on this device opens so you can tick what else to bring.

Receive updates only

For a player nobody edits on, such as a meditation room's laptop, turn on Receive updates only. That device takes every change from the shared library and sends nothing. Anything changed on it by accident is replaced at the next sync.

Leaving

Leave shared library stops syncing this device. Its library stays exactly as it is now, as an ordinary library of its own.

If something goes wrong

  • Sync log: Settings → Shared library → Sync log lists what syncing did recently: each file sent or received, what it saved, and any errors, with a line every 10 minutes while 37 Player is open. It's kept on this device even if 37 Player closes or crashes, so a gap in those lines shows when it stopped. Copy it into a message if you're reporting a problem.
  • Going round in circles: if this device saves to the shared library 30 times in 2 minutes, syncing stops by itself and says so. Sync now starts it again.
  • Opening without syncing: add ?nosync to the end of 37 Player's address (for example https://37player.com/37-player.html?nosync). Sharing stays off for that session, and Settings lets you leave the shared library.

topics.title: Libraries
topics.bodyHtml:
One device can hold more than one library: a Center's library and your own, say, or your Dharma recordings and everything else. Each library has its own tracks, playlists, backups, PIN and sharing. Only one is open at a time, and switching never loses anything: the others are simply put aside until you open them again.

Making one

In Settings → Switch libraries, choose New library…, give it a name, and choose how it starts:

  • Start empty: a new, empty library. Fill it as usual, with Import / Export.
  • Join a shared library: enter the join code and this device's name, and the new library joins straight away. Leave the name empty and it takes the shared library's own name, such as "IKRC Library".

Joining a shared library from a library that already has tracks asks first whether to make a new library for it instead. That's usually the right choice: joining with an existing library would add all its tracks and playlists to the shared library, for everyone in it to see.

Switching

Once there's more than one library, the open library's name is shown in the top bar, so it's clear which one a session is about to play from. Click it to see the others and switch. Settings → Switch libraries can switch too, and it's where libraries are renamed and deleted.

If something is playing, switching asks first, because it stops playback. Each library remembers its own place: the playlist you had open and where the session had got to.

Two windows can have two different libraries open at the same time. A new window opens the library chosen most recently.

What belongs to each library, and what to the device

  • Each library has its own: tracks and playlists, the PIN, the backup folder, the File format settings, and its shared library, if any, with What's on this device, Review changes and Receive updates only.
  • The device keeps for all of them: the language, display settings, the screen-off playback settings, this device's name for shared libraries, and the converter.

Syncing

Only the open library syncs. A shared library that isn't open catches up as soon as you open it, with whatever changed meanwhile, so nothing is missed.

Deleting

Settings → Switch libraries → Delete… removes a library's tracks, playlists and settings from this device. If it keeps a backup folder (Chrome or Edge on a computer), the dialog offers to delete that backup too: only the files 37 Player put there, and only while the folder still holds that library's backup. Backup files the browser saved (Firefox, Safari, phones) can't be reached, so delete them yourself if you no longer want them; their names include the library's name, such as lib-native-backup-full-skbc-2026-10-22-1530.zip (backups made before version 1.4.051 don't). The shared library it may be joined to isn't touched either: other devices keep it, and this device can join it again later. To keep a copy first, open the library and make a backup or a Portable export.

The open library can't be deleted: switch to another one first.

Space

All libraries share the browser's storage on this device. A recording in two libraries is stored twice.

topics.title: Phones and tablets
topics.bodyHtml:
iPad and iPhone: start from the Home Screen

Safari on an iPad or iPhone erases a website's data after 7 days without a visit, and the library with it. A 37 Player added to the Home Screen keeps its library. It's a separate app with a library of its own, so do this before importing anything:

  1. In Safari, open 37 Player and tap the Share button (a square with an arrow pointing up), then View More. If Share isn't showing, tap ••• first.
  2. Choose Add to Home Screen. Leave Open as Web App turned on: turned off, the icon only opens the website in Safari, with Safari's library and its 7-day limit. Then tap Add.
  3. Open 37 Player from the Home Screen, and set it up there.

Already built a library in Safari? Use 'Import / Export' → Export there, then Import in the Home Screen app.

Android: install it as an app

In Chrome on Android, 37 Player offers to install itself when it first opens; otherwise use Chrome's ⋮ menu → Add to Home screen or Install app. The installed app and the website share one library, and Chrome keeps an installed app's data safe rather than clearing it when space runs low.

Touch

On a touch screen, 'Edit Playlists' and the 'Library' work by tapping and holding instead of clicking and dragging.

Selecting

  • Tap a track to select it. Its ✎ and ✕ show once it's selected.
  • Hold, then slide up or down to select a run of tracks.
  • Tap a folder to open or close it. Its Print, ✎ and ✕ show on the folder you tapped last.

Moving

  • Tracks: select them, then hold a selected track until it lifts (about half a second) and slide it to where it should go. From the right-hand column, this copies tracks into the playlist being edited.
  • Folders and playlists in the first column: hold one until it lifts, then slide it onto a folder to put it inside, or between two rows to move it there. The bar under the list moves it to the very end.
  • Near the top or bottom edge, the column scrolls by itself.

Copy and paste work too, from the bar above each list.

Column widths

On a tablet, drag the thin line between two columns to make a column wider, such as the right-hand one, so long titles can be read. Turning on Wrap long titles in Display settings (◐) shows titles in full on every row.

On a phone, the screen slides sideways between the columns. Drag the thin line at a column's right-hand edge with a finger to make that column wider or narrower (up to nine tenths of the screen, so its line always shows); the columns to its right just move along. The widths are kept for next time, separately for holding the phone upright and on its side. To put every column back as it started, use Reset column widths at the bottom of Display settings (◐).

Playing with the screen off

A playlist keeps playing with the screen locked or while you use another app, and moves from track to track by itself. While the screen is off, 37 Player also plays a silent sound alongside the track. Without it, Android lets a track that starts with the screen off play for a couple of seconds and then silences it.

If playback ever goes quiet while the time keeps moving, open Settings → Playback → Playback log afterwards. It records when each track started, when the app left and came back to the screen, and whether the phone stopped or paused anything. Copy it into a message when reporting the problem.

At a stop, the lock screen keeps showing the stop's name with a ▶. Pressing it, there or on headphones, continues the session without unlocking. The same after pausing with the screen locked: the paused track stays on the lock screen, and ▶ carries on from where it was. For that, 37 Player plays silence while it waits: through a stop for as long as it lasts, after a pause for up to 30 minutes. That uses a little battery. To save battery, turn off Keep the lock screen ready at stops and pauses in Settings → Playback; then carry on from 37 Player itself.

topics.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
topics.bodyHtml:
A few keys work everywhere: Escape closes whatever dialog is open, and Enter inside any dialog's text field submits it.

Playing

EnterStarts a track from the beginning — the highlighted one if there is one, otherwise whatever's currently queued. With another playlist open over the playing one, it starts that playlist instead: its highlighted track, or else its first.
EscapeCloses another playlist opened over the playing one, without changing anything.
SpaceToggles play/pause.
Double-click a trackPlays it immediately, stopping whatever was playing before.

Edit Playlists

SpaceToggles play/pause on the main transport.
Ctrl/Cmd+CCopies the selected track(s), silence(s), or stop(s) from whichever pane (the playlist being edited, or the one being browsed alongside it) was last clicked into.
Ctrl/Cmd+VPastes the copied items into the playlist currently being edited. Audio files copied in your computer's file manager can be pasted too — into the playlist (before the first selected entry, or at the end), or on 'Library' as an import — in browsers and systems that pass copied files on to web pages; otherwise, drag them in.
Delete / BackspaceRemoves the selected item(s) from the playlist being edited. Only acts there — the browse-only pane alongside it is unaffected.
EEdits the selected track, silence, or stop, in whichever pane was last clicked into.

Library

SpaceToggles play/pause — the previewed track if one is loaded, otherwise the main transport.
EnterPlays the first selected track.
Delete / BackspaceDeletes the selected track(s), with confirmation.
↑ / ↓Moves the selection within whichever list — Artists, Albums, or Tracks — was last clicked. Only when exactly one item is selected there.
EEdits the selected track(s), or renames the selected artist/album across every track that uses it.

None of these are active while a dialog is open, or while typing in a text field.
